title: Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs
hookLine: trading communities, like Makhan Shah and Lakhi Shah

lines: A LIFE AS A TRADING JOURNEY.
cards: Guru Nanak sometimes speaks to the listener as a trader.
In one hymn he calls the listener vanjaria mitra, my merchant friend, and walks them through the night of a life watch by watch, as if it were a long trading journey. What are you carrying home?
The image would land in a world of traders: caravans of pack bullocks, boats on the rivers, goods moving from market to market. Some of those trading families became Sikhs.
Two of them did something the panth still remembers.

teach.b: The Lubanas and the Vanjaras are trading communities, remembered for carrying goods across long distances by caravan and by boat.
Both have Sikh families with deep roots in the panth, and Sikh tradition keeps two of their names close. First, Makhan Shah Lubana.

The story says his ship was caught in a storm, and he vowed an offering of gold to the Guru if he came through. He did. When he went to pay his vow, he found a crowd of men each claiming to be the Guru.

So he tried a quiet test: he laid a small offering before each claimant, and each accepted it. Then he came to a man sitting apart in meditation, Tegh Bahadur, who said, in effect: you promised more than this.

teach.h: MAKHAN SHAH FINDS THE HIDDEN GURU.
teach.b: Makhan Shah ran up to a rooftop and shouted that he had found the Guru. Second, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, and the story turns darker.
After Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi, his body lay where the authorities had left it.

teach.h: LAKHI SHAH GIVES UP HIS HOUSE.
teach.b: Tradition says Lakhi Shah, a carrier with carts and men, brought his caravan through, took the body away in the confusion, carried it home, and set his own house alight so the Guru could be cremated with honor without drawing attention.
A gurdwara stands at that place today.

teach.h: ANG 74: WHAT DOES THE TRADER CARRY HOME?
teach.b: One trader found a hidden Guru; one gave up his own house for him.

Guru Nanak's merchant hymn, on Ang 74, follows the trader through the watches of the night to the journey's end. In the panth's memory, these two spent their journeys on the Guru, and it still says their names.

how: Sikhs remember Makhan Shah Lubana and Lakhi Shah Vanjara in the stories of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and Lubana and Vanjara Sikh families keep their trading heritage alongside their place in the panth.

games.q: what does “lubana and vanjara sikhs” mean?
o: Sikhs from the hill clans who guarded the Gurus
Sikhs from trading communities of caravans and boats
Sikhs from priestly families who kept the shrines

games.q: inside the traders: tap the pairs.
p: a life as a trading journey

s: Makhan Shah found only one man claiming to be the Guru
he found a crowd of claimants, and tested them with a quiet offering.
tradition says Lakhi Shah cremated Guru Tegh Bahadur by setting his own house alight
he carried the body home and burned his house so the Guru was cremated with honor.
Guru Nanak calls the listener a merchant friend in one hymn
on Ang 74 he walks the merchant friend through the night of a life.

games.q: you're Makhan Shah, come to pay your vow. a crowd of men each say they're the Guru. what do you do?
o: give the full vow to the first man you meet.
lay a small offering before each and wait.
go home and keep the gold.
games.why: each claimant accepted the small offering. only Tegh Bahadur said, in effect, you promised more. Makhan Shah ran to the roof to shout that he'd found the Guru.

practice: Call up one person whose work is buying and selling, carrying and delivering, a shopkeeper you know by face, a driver who brings things to your door, and think of the roads and hours behind what you need.
Breathe in and see their face; breathe out and hold a plain thank-you ready, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs. Sikhs from trading communities, among them Makhan Shah, who found the Guru, and Lakhi Shah, who gave up his house for him. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a trader or merchant; Guru Nanak calls the listener vanjaria, merchant friend.

carryVoice: Your line: the traders. Two journeys, and both were spent on the Guru. That's today, done.
